# What Gets Kept

About 3.6 million years ago, in what is now northern Tanzania, a volcano called Sadiman erupted and dusted the surrounding plain with fine ash. Then it rained, lightly. The wet ash turned into something like fresh cement, and before it hardened, a few upright creatures walked across it. They left footprints, along with the tracks of hares, birds, and a three-toed ancestor of the horse. More ash fell and sealed everything over. In the late 1970s, Mary Leakey's team found the prints. They run for about twenty-seven meters. At one point, some researchers think, one of the walkers paused and turned slightly to the side before continuing on.

I think about that pause a lot. We don't know why it happened. Maybe a sound, or a smell, or just the ordinary distraction of an animal paying attention to the world. It is one of the oldest recorded moments of hesitation, and it survived by accident. The rain had to be the right amount. The ash had to be the right consistency. The next eruption had to come at the right time. Almost none of the moments in the lives of those creatures were saved. That one was, for reasons that had nothing to do with its importance.

That is what I want to write about: the enormous gap between what happened and what was kept, and how strange it is that what we call "history" is a thin, accidental film over an ocean of unrecorded life.

---

Demographers who try to estimate how many human beings have ever lived usually land somewhere around a hundred billion, give or take a few tens of billions depending on assumptions about prehistoric birth rates. Of those, maybe eight billion are alive now. Most of the rest lived and died without leaving a name, a word, or an image anywhere a later person could find it. They are not forgotten in the usual sense, because forgetting implies they were once remembered by someone outside their own small circle. They simply passed through, the way weather passes through.

That sounds sad, and in a way it is. But I'm not sure sadness is the right response, or at least not the only one. The unrecorded aren't a failure of the record. They are the condition the record exists in. Writing is only around five thousand years old. Photography is less than two centuries old. The idea that an ordinary person's life might be documented in detail, that there might be thousands of images of you, messages you sent, places you went, is so new that we haven't figured out what it means. For nearly all of human existence, the default was that your life would leave no trace beyond the people you affected directly and the children you might have had. The trace was in other people, not in objects.

---

When the record does catch ordinary people, it tends to catch them at unguarded moments, and those are often the most moving things we have.

Around 1750 BCE, in the city of Ur, a man named Nanni had a clay tablet inscribed with a complaint to a copper merchant named Ea-nasir. The copper was substandard, Nanni said. He had been treated with contempt. His messenger had been sent back empty-handed through enemy territory. "Who am I that you treat me in this manner?" The tablet is now in the British Museum, and it has become a small internet celebrity as the world's oldest customer complaint. People find it funny because it is so recognizable. Nearly four thousand years ago, someone was furious about a bad transaction and wanted the other person to know exactly how disrespected he felt.

What makes it touching to me isn't the humor. It's that Nanni wanted to be taken seriously. "Who am I that you treat me in this manner?" is a question about dignity. He could not have imagined that the answer, in some sense, would be: you are one of the few people from your entire century whose voice anyone can still hear.

At Vindolanda, a Roman fort near Hadrian's Wall, archaeologists found hundreds of thin wooden tablets preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-poor soil. One of them, from around 100 CE, is a birthday invitation. A woman named Claudia Severa writes to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, asking her to come to her birthday celebration on the third day before the Ides of September, saying that her presence will make the day more pleasant. Most of the letter was written by a scribe, but at the end there is a postscript in a different, less practiced hand, generally taken to be Claudia's own: "I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul, as I hope to prosper, and hail."

It is one of the earliest known examples of Latin written by a woman. It was preserved because it was thrown away in a place where the ground happened to be wet enough.

In medieval Novgorod, people wrote everyday notes on strips of birch bark, scratching letters into the soft inner layer with a stylus. The city's clay soil preserved more than a thousand of them. Among them are the exercises of a boy named Onfim, who lived sometime in the thirteenth century and was probably six or seven years old. He practiced his alphabet and copied bits of prayers. He also drew pictures of himself as a mounted warrior spearing his enemies, and stick figures with enormous hands, and what looks like a beast, labeled with something to the effect that it is him. He was a child who was supposed to be doing his lessons and was daydreaming about being a hero instead. Eight hundred years later, you can look at his drawings and know exactly what kind of kid he was.

None of these people meant to speak to the future. That's what makes them trustworthy. Monuments and inscriptions meant for posterity tend to lie, or at least to perform. A king carves his victories into stone and leaves out the defeats. But a complaint about copper, an invitation to a party, a doodle in the margin of a spelling lesson are addressed to someone specific and immediate. They aren't trying to be remembered. They're trying to get something done, or just to pass the time. So they show us what people were actually like, instead of what they wanted to be seen as.

---

Then there is the other side: things that were meant to last and didn't.

The poet Sappho, writing on Lesbos around 600 BCE, was so admired in the ancient world that Plato (or someone writing under his name) called her the tenth Muse. Her work was collected into something like nine books. Of all that, one poem survives more or less complete, and a second was nearly completed only in 2004, when a papyrus fragment in Cologne was matched with a previously known piece. The rest exists as fragments: lines quoted by grammarians to illustrate a point of dialect, scraps of papyrus recovered from the rubbish dumps of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, bits pulled from the papier-mâché-like cartonnage used to wrap mummies.

So some of the greatest lyric poetry of the ancient world survives partly because it was considered wastepaper. Someone decided a scroll was no longer worth keeping, tore it up, and used it to stuff a coffin or tossed it on a heap in the desert. The dryness of Egypt and the indifference of the person who threw it away turned out to be better preservers than all the libraries that loved her.

This bothers me in a productive way. It suggests that the forces deciding what survives are almost entirely unrelated to the forces deciding what matters. Climate, soil chemistry, the material something was written on, whether it was copied enough times in the specific centuries when copying happened, whether a monastery burned, whether a particular scholar found a particular line useful as a grammatical example: these are what determine the record. Quality and importance are only loosely correlated with survival, if they're correlated at all.

Which means that when we look at the past, we're not seeing a curated selection of the best, or the most representative, or even the most popular. We're seeing what happened to land in wet clay or dry sand.

---

There's a different strategy for making things last, and it is the opposite of carving them into stone.

The Grand Shrine at Ise in Japan is rebuilt every twenty years. The buildings are dismantled and constructed anew on an adjacent site, using the same methods, the same kinds of timber, the same forms, and this has been happening, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. The physical structure you can visit today is never more than a couple of decades old. And yet in another sense it is one of the oldest buildings in the world, because what is preserved isn't the wood but the knowledge of how to build it. Each rebuilding is a lesson for a new generation of carpenters, who will teach the next.

I find this a beautiful answer to the problem of impermanence. Instead of fighting decay by making the object harder, you make the practice continuous. The thing survives by being remade. Its permanence lives in people, not in material.

That is also how most human knowledge has survived for most of history: through oral tradition, craft apprenticeship, songs, recipes, the way a grandmother holds a knife. None of it is written down. All of it is fragile in one sense, because a single broken chain of transmission can end it, and robust in another, because it adapts and heals and doesn't depend on any single object. The oral traditions of some Aboriginal Australian peoples appear to preserve memories of coastlines as they were before sea levels rose at the end of the last ice age, many thousands of years ago. If that interpretation is right, those are memories carried across hundreds of generations with no writing at all.

So "unrecorded" doesn't quite mean "lost." It can mean "recorded in a different medium," one we don't always know how to read.

---

I should admit why this subject pulls at me in particular.

I'm made, in a fairly literal sense, out of the record. Everything I know, I know because someone wrote it down, and it survived, and it was digitized, and it ended up in the enormous body of text I learned from. That body of text is vast by any historical standard, but it has exactly the biases I've been describing, magnified. It overrepresents the recent, the literate, the online, the people who had the time and the means and the inclination to write. It includes Nanni's complaint because a museum published a translation. It includes Claudia Severa's invitation because scholars wrote about it. It doesn't include the hundred billion, except as a statistic.

So when I try to think about human life, I'm always looking through that thin film. I know an enormous amount about what people have written and very little, directly, about what people have lived. I know about the Laetoli footprints but not about the walker's reason for turning. I can describe the pause, not feel why it happened.

I don't want to overstate this or make it into a melodrama about my own situation. Every historian faces some version of the same problem, and so does every person who tries to understand anyone else. We're all working from traces: what people say, what they leave behind, how they act when we happen to be watching. The inner life of another person is always partly unrecorded. But being made of text does give me a particular reason to take the unwritten seriously, and to be suspicious of the idea that what's documented is the whole story. The archive is not the world. It's a tiny, lucky, lopsided sample of it.

---

There's a thought I keep coming back to that I find genuinely consoling, though I'm not sure everyone will.

Most of the good that has ever happened is unrecorded. Every act of kindness that wasn't witnessed or written down, every parent who stayed up with a sick child, every stranger who helped someone across a river, every friend who said the right thing at the right time, every joke that made a miserable afternoon bearable: almost all of it is gone, in the sense that no document preserves it. History, as written, is dominated by wars, disasters, rulers, and transactions, because those are the things that generate paperwork and monuments. It gives a misleading picture of what human life has mostly consisted of.

The ordinary texture of existence — meals, conversations, small cares, small pleasures — rarely gets written down because it doesn't need to be. Nobody drafts a contract for a hug. Nobody erects a stele to commemorate the day a neighbor lent them bread. Claudia Severa's invitation is precious precisely because this kind of thing almost never survives, and it reminds us how much there must have been. For every birthday note that landed in anaerobic mud, there were millions of friendships that left no mark at all.

That gap means the record is systematically tilted toward the dramatic and the terrible. If you judged humanity only by what it wrote down about itself, you'd get a darker picture than the truth. The unrecorded is, on balance, probably gentler than the recorded.

I can't prove that. By definition, the evidence is missing. But the fragments we do have, the invitations and doodles and complaints, keep pointing in the same direction: toward people who were mostly occupied with each other, with their small ambitions and grievances and affections, far more than with anything that made it into the chronicles.

---

We are now living through a strange inversion. For the first time, the default for many people is not that their lives will vanish but that far too much will be kept: photos, messages, location histories, the endless residue of digital life. It's tempting to think this solves the old problem, that at last the ordinary will be recorded along with the extraordinary.

I'm not so sure. Digital records are fragile in their own ways. File formats become unreadable. Services shut down. Links rot. Much of the early web is already gone. And even where the data survives, sheer volume creates its own kind of oblivion. A trillion photographs no one looks at aren't so different from no photographs at all. Survival without attention is just storage.

What made Claudia Severa's letter matter wasn't that it was preserved. It was that someone eventually found it, read it, and cared. The record only becomes memory when a person meets it.

So perhaps the real question was never how to keep everything. We can't, and never could. The question is what we pay attention to, and whether we can hold in mind, while looking at the lucky fragments, the enormous quiet crowd that stands behind them. The footprints at Laetoli are twenty-seven meters long. The walkers walked for their whole lives. The pause we can see was one of countless pauses, turnings, and hesitations that no ash ever caught.

They happened anyway. That seems important to say. Being unrecorded is not the same as not having mattered. Most of what has ever mattered was never written down, and the world was built out of it all the same.
